newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries open softer, Humphrey-Hawkins fears.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries open softer, Humphrey-Hawkins fears.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries opened weaker on Monday, as investors continued to book profits ahead of this week's Humphrey-Hawkins testimony.
In early trading, the 30-year bond was at 101-2/32, down 6/32 from late Friday. Its yield rose to 6.54 percent from 6.52 percent.

With no economic news slated for release on Monday, the market is firmly focused on Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's testimony to Congress, beginning on Tuesday. Traders said the market is fearful Greenspan may spook the markets with talk of rising inflationary pressures.

Greenspan "is a wildcard and could be scary," said Jim Caron, a trader at Sanwa Securities Co. "People are nervous what he has to say. If he says the same old story, we could go right back up, but why take the risk?"
Numerous accounts opted to take profits during the London session during the night -- Tokyo was closed for a holiday -- in a continuation of the profit-taking seen in the U.S. on Friday.
Most of the selling took place in 10-year notes, traders noted.
"People are hedging themselves," Caron said. "The market went up too far, too fast. We are now backing and filling."

That does not mean the market's rally is over, traders said. Once Greenspan's testimony is done and the market gets past the two- and five-year note auctions this week, prices could rise again if it is believed the Fed is on hold indefinitely.

Along with the position squaring ahead of Humprey-Hawkins, some noted the market may build in concessions for the two-year note sale on Tuesday and five-year note auction on Wednesday. A combined $27 billion is up for sale.
Later Monday, the Treasury will sell $16.0 billion of three- and six-month bills. Demand, as usual, is seen very good.
In early when-issued trading, the three-month bill was at 5.12 percent, while the six-month bill was at 5.17 percent.
As for outstanding issues, the two-year note was at 100-5/32, down 1/32, to yield 5.91 percent.
Five-year notes were down 3/32 to 100-11/32, yielding 6.17 and 10-year notes were down 5/32 to 102-19/32, yielding 6.27 percent.
